Title: Did you really see this word?
Hook (spoken): Why will you remember 1 word you never saw?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. I will prove it.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why will you remember 1 word you never saw? | Wait for the last part. I will prove it. | [pause 0.6] | Read these words once, and try to remember them. | [pause 6.5] | Was the word sleep on the list? | [pause 1.0] | Look again, because it was never there! | [pause 1.2] | Your brain saw bed and dream, and added sleep. | In one test, people recalled it about half the time. | Did you see sleep on the list?
Frame 0: A word list sliding past on a bedroom wall; Spark holds up a pillow, sure of himself
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick pins up the list and whispers. Spark brags that he remembers everything, then shouts SLEEP!
First payoff (by ~10 s): The question: was sleep on the list? Spark says yes.
Reveal: The list rolls back, word by word. There is no SLEEP. The word falls off Spark's memory wall and smashes.
World: Night-blue bedroom with one long wall
Comment question: Did you see sleep on the list?
Claim + numbers: Lists of related words make people recall a word that was never shown. Exp 2, 15-word lists: false recall 55%, a rate across lists. Show the 15-word sleep list on screen.
Caveat: One lab test with students; 55% is a rate across lists.
Flags: Show bed, rest, awake, tired, dream, wake, night, blanket, doze, slumber, snore, pillow, peace, yawn, drowsy. Words on screen, not spoken.

Title: Is there a hole in your eye?
Hook (spoken): Why can your eye never see this 1 spot?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. One dot will disappear.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why can your eye never see this 1 spot? | Wait for the last part. One dot will disappear. | [pause 0.6] | Close your left eye, and look at the left dot. | Now move your phone slowly towards your face. | [pause 3.5] | Did the right dot disappear for you? | [pause 0.8] | That dot landed on your blind spot. | Each eye has one small place that cannot see. | Your brain fills the gap, so you never notice. | Did the dot disappear for you?
Frame 0: Two big dots; Spark covers one eye, the other eye huge
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark says his eyes are perfect. Mr. Trick steals a dot from the wall in front of him.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The right dot disappears as the viewer moves closer.
Reveal: The eye opens in cross-section: the gap where no vision happens, and the brain paints over it.
World: Optician's room, eye chart on the wall
Comment question: Did the dot disappear for you?
Claim + numbers: Each eye has a blind spot about 15 degrees from centre, about 5 degrees wide; the brain fills it in.
Caveat: Tell viewers to move slowly, because the distance differs. Phones only.
Flags: Dots about 5.5 cm apart on a phone (about 20 cm viewing, my calculation). Will not work on TV or tablet (about 20% of watch time). Owner tests on a real phone first.

Title: Can your eyes paint a colour that is not there?
Hook (spoken): Why do you see 1 colour that is never there?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. Spark will get his colour back.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you see 1 colour that is never there? | Wait for the last part. Spark will get his colour back. | [pause 0.5] | Stare at the black dot for ten seconds, and do not move. | [pause 10.0] | Now look at this white wall, and keep still. | [pause 2.5] | That colour is not on your screen right now! | Your eyes got tired, so white looks roughly opposite. | What colour did you see on the wall?
Frame 0: Spark filled solid orange-red, one black dot on his chest, nervous face
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick has painted Spark red and stolen his teal. The viewer's eyes will bring it back.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The screen turns white with a thin Spark outline; the colour ghost appears.
Reveal: The viewer sees a ghost Spark in a colour that is not on the screen, close to his real colour.
World: Plain paint shop, one big white wall
Claim + numbers: Staring at a colour leaves a roughly opposite, paler colour on white. Studies used 20-30 s stares.
Caveat: Say roughly opposite, not exact. No source gives a minimum stare, so 10 s is untested.
Flags: Owner must test on a real phone. If 10 s is too weak, raise it to 15-18 s and allow up to 40 s. Static picture during the stare, no flashing.

Title: Are these two squares really the same colour?
Hook (spoken): Why do you never see these 2 squares match?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. I will join them together.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you never see these 2 squares match? | Wait for the last part. I will join them together. | [pause 0.6] | Square A looks dark, and square B looks light. | But watch what happens when the board goes away. | [pause 1.0] | They are exactly the same grey colour! | [pause 1.2] | Your brain sees a shadow, and it corrects for it. | This helps you read the real world every day. | Did you believe that they matched?
Frame 0: Checkerboard with a shadow across it, A and B marked; Spark laughs at the idea
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark bets his bulb that B is lighter. Mr. Trick takes the bet.
First payoff (by ~10 s): A grey bar slides from A to B, and the board fades away.
Reveal: With the board gone, both squares are one grey. Spark's bulb is carried off.
World: Original board in a games room
Claim + numbers: Squares A and B are the same grey.
Caveat: Credit: based on Adelson's checker-shadow illusion. Adelson argues this shows vision working well.
Flags: Draw our own board. Check pixel values after final encoding.

Title: Would you notice if the person talking to you changed?
Hook (spoken): Why would you never notice 1 stranger being swapped?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. A door does the trick.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why would you never notice 1 stranger being swapped? | Wait for the last part. A door does the trick. | [pause 0.5] | A man asked strangers on a campus for directions. | Then two men carried a door between them. | Behind the door, a different man took his place. | [pause 1.0] | About half the people did not notice him change! | [pause 1.0] | It was a small test, with only fifteen people. | Your brain keeps less detail than it feels. | Would you have noticed the new man?
Frame 0: Stranger with a map, a door coming in from the side, Spark squinting
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark gives directions confidently while Mr. Trick carries the door. Spark never notices the swap.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Behind the door the two men swap.
Reveal: Replay from above: door passes, man A walks off, man B keeps talking, Spark still chatting.
Claim + numbers: Exp 1: 7 of 15 noticed, 8 did not. Noticers were students aged about 20-30.
Caveat: Very small test. Say about half, never most.

Title: Can you pass this simple colour test?
Hook (spoken): You fail this 1 colour test. Can you stop reading?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. It gets much harder.
Voice script (rows split by |): You fail this 1 colour test. Can you stop reading? | Wait for the last part. It gets much harder. | [pause 0.5] | Say each colour out loud, and do not read. | [pause 3.0] | Now try these words, and say only the colour. | [pause 4.5] | Did your mouth get stuck on the word? | [pause 0.8] | Your brain reads the word before you can stop it. | In the old test, people became much slower. | Which word stopped you just now?
Frame 0: The word RED in green letters, Spark with his mouth open and stuck
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark races through the easy round, then trips over every word in round two.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Round one is easy. Round two, the viewer stumbles.
Reveal: Spark's mouth jams on the word, and a giant word falls on him.
Claim + numbers: Stroop Exp 2: 100 students, 63.3 s for squares vs 110.3 s for conflicting words per 100 responses (74% longer).
Caveat: 74% is the 1935 card test.
Flags: Colour-blind viewers may not be able to play.

Title: Could you miss a gorilla right in front of you?
Hook (spoken): How can you miss 1 gorilla in front of you?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. Even doctors missed one.
Voice script (rows split by |): How can you miss 1 gorilla in front of you? | Wait for the last part. Even doctors missed one. | [pause 0.5] | People counted ball passes in a short video. | A person in a gorilla suit walked through the game. | About half of the people did not see it. | So scientists hid a gorilla in some lung scans. | [pause 1.0] | Twenty of twenty-four doctors missed it! | [pause 1.0] | Your eyes can look, and your brain can miss. | Did you see the gorilla coming?
Frame 0: A chest scan with a tiny gorilla shape inside; Spark's face close to it, not seeing
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark counts passes with a clicker while a gorilla suit walks behind him.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The gorilla walks through and most of Spark's attention stays on the ball.
Reveal: The lung scan grows to fill the screen: a gorilla shape inside it, with 20 OF 24 DOCTORS.
World: Basketball court, then a dark scan screen on its wall
Comment question: Did you see the gorilla coming?
Claim + numbers: Simons & Chabris: 46% missed across events, 56% gorilla only (secondhand). Drew: 20 of 24 radiologists missed it; 12 of those 20 looked straight at it.
Caveat: Doctors were searching for lung spots, and they still found more spots than untrained people. Only 24 doctors.
Flags: Re-check Simons numbers in the primary paper on the day. Our own drawing, never the original video.

Title: How many Fs can you count?
Hook (spoken): How many letters will you miss in this 1 sentence?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. I will show you where.
Voice script (rows split by |): How many letters will you miss in this 1 sentence? | Wait for the last part. I will show you where. | [pause 0.5] | Count every letter F in this sentence. | [pause 5.0] | Spark counted three, but there are six. | [pause 1.0] | Look at the small word of, three times! | [pause 1.0] | Readers often miss letters in small common words. | Scientists still debate the exact reason for this. | How many Fs did you count?
Frame 0: A sentence on a blackboard, Spark holding up three fingers proudly
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark answers THREE, slams the chalk. Mr. Trick adds up behind him.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The answer: there are six.
Reveal: Three small OF words light up, one by one, each with an F Spark missed.
Comment question: How many Fs did you count?
Claim + numbers: Missing-letter effect: in Healy's passage, 'the' held 28% of the t's but 62% of missed t's. Sentence has 6 Fs (counted).
Caveat: The research used passages, not this sentence, whose origin is unknown.
Flags: Never present the sentence as a study. Do not repeat the 'v sound' explanation.

Title: Are these two tables really different?
Hook (spoken): Why would you lose a bet on these 2 tables?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. I will turn one.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why would you lose a bet on these 2 tables? | Wait for the last part. I will turn one. | [pause 0.5] | The left table looks long and very thin. | The right table looks short and much wider. | Now I remove the legs, and turn one top. | [pause 1.0] | They are exactly the same shape! | [pause 1.2] | Your brain sees depth in a flat picture. | So it stretches one table without asking you. | Which table would you buy from me?
Frame 0: Two table tops, Spark with a tape measure tangled round him
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark tries to sell the long table for double. Mr. Trick lifts the top off.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Legs vanish; one top starts to turn.
Reveal: The turned top lands exactly on the other, and they match.
Claim + numbers: Top surfaces are the same shape, one rotated 90 degrees.
Caveat: Only the tops match, not the legs. Credit Shepard.
Flags: Build the geometry exactly, then check the overlay in a still.

Title: Would you defend a choice you never made?
Hook (spoken): Why would you defend 1 choice you never made?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. People did this in a test.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why would you defend 1 choice you never made? | Wait for the last part. People did this in a test. | [pause 0.5] | People picked the better looking face from two photos. | Then a scientist handed them the chosen photo. | But he had secretly swapped it with a card trick. | [pause 1.0] | Only about one person in eight noticed right away! | [pause 1.0] | Then they explained why they liked that face. | So your reason may come after your choice. | Would you have noticed the swap?
Frame 0: Two face cards in a hand, one being swapped; Spark grinning, sure
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick does the card trick. Spark explains at length why he loves the face he did not pick.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Spark is handed the wrong face.
Reveal: Rewind shows the swap. Spark's speech bubble of reasons collapses.
Comment question: Would you have noticed the swap?
Claim + numbers: 118 people, 354 swapped trials. 13% detected at the moment, at most 26% by any measure.
Caveat: Face photos, not big life decisions.
Flags: Check replications on the day. Invented faces only.

Title: Can one thing feel like two?
Hook (spoken): Why do your 2 fingers feel what is never there?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. You can try it now.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do your 2 fingers feel what is never there? | Wait for the last part. You can try it now. | [pause 0.5] | Cross two fingers on one hand, just like this. | Now touch a small round thing with both tips. | [pause 3.5] | Does that one thing feel like two now? | [pause 0.8] | Those two sides of your fingers never normally meet. | So your brain decides there must be two things. | Did you feel two things or one?
Frame 0: Two crossed fingers, huge, a small round ball between them; Spark seeing double
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark crosses his fingers and starts looking for the second ball everywhere.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The viewer feels two.
Reveal: Skin map: those two outer sides never normally touch one thing, so the brain says TWO.
World: Toy shop with a shelf of balls
Claim + numbers: Crossed fingers: about 93% 'two' vs 16.7% with parallel fingers (blindfolded).
Caveat: Small clinical sample, so no number on screen. Do not state the explanation as settled.

Title: Did you just miss a word?
Hook (spoken): How did you never see this 1 extra word?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. It is right in front of you.
Voice script (rows split by |): How did you never see this 1 extra word? | Wait for the last part. It is right in front of you. | [pause 0.5] | Read the sign once, and tell me what it says. | [pause 3.0] | Now look closely, because the word the is there twice. | [pause 1.0] | In one lab test, readers noticed less than half the time! | [pause 1.0] | Scientists are still working out why this happens. | Did you see the extra word?
Frame 0: A sign with a sentence that has THE THE across a line break; Spark reads it with a finger
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick slips an extra word in. Spark reads it aloud without noticing.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The second THE lights up.
Reveal: Spark looks back at everything he has read, every sign now with an extra THE.
Comment question: Did you see the extra word?
Claim + numbers: Staub et al.: 51 people, 36 items: repeated 'the' noticed 45.8%, repeated noun 90.2%.
Caveat: Lab sentences. Do not call it repetition blindness.
Flags: Sign wording chosen by the run, e.g. a line break between the two words. Hook is said before the sign is read.

Title: Would you have believed this horse could do maths?
Hook (spoken): Why would you never doubt 1 horse doing maths?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. One small test exposed him.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why would you never doubt 1 horse doing maths? | Wait for the last part. One small test exposed him. | [pause 0.5] | In Germany, Hans tapped his hoof to give answers. | Experts looked for a trick and found nothing. | Then a scientist tried one simple new thing. | The person asking did not know the answer. | [pause 1.0] | Now Hans was almost always wrong! | [pause 1.0] | He had been reading tiny head movements all along. | Do you give away answers with your face?
Frame 0: A horse tapping a hoof at a chalkboard, Spark clapping and amazed
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark is Hans's biggest fan and buys the T-shirt. Mr. Trick does not appear: nobody meant to trick anyone.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Hans answers correctly in front of a crowd.
Reveal: A curtain hides the answer from the questioner; the horse keeps tapping, and is wrong, again and again.
Comment question: Do you give away answers with your face?
Claim + numbers: Numerals: 98% right when questioner knew (42 tests), 8% when not (49). Pfungst investigated; cues unintentional.
Caveat: No fraud. His owner did not know.
Flags: Generic labelled figures only.

Title: Can a room make you grow?
Hook (spoken): Why do you see 1 person grow before your eyes?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. I will open the roof.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you see 1 person grow before your eyes? | Wait for the last part. I will open the roof. | [pause 0.5] | Spark walks slowly from one corner to the other. | He gets much bigger with every single step. | But look through the hole, and the room looks normal. | [pause 1.0] | From above, the walls and floor are crooked! | [pause 1.0] | One corner is much farther away from you. | Your brain trusts the room, and changes the person. | Would you walk into this room?
Frame 0: Spark huge in one corner of a checked room, a tiny Spark in the other
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick builds the room and invites Spark to stroll. Spark grows and thinks he is a giant.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Spark walks across and grows.
Reveal: Camera lifts through the ceiling: the room is a crooked wedge, one corner much farther away.
Comment question: Would you walk into this room?
Claim + numbers: Ames room: looks normal from one viewing point with one eye; people seem to change size.
Caveat: Works from one point only. No year on screen, because sources differ.
Flags: Best use of the camera rig: build the wedge in true perspective.

Title: How many people does it take to share a birthday?
Hook (spoken): Why do you never guess this 1 birthday number?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. The answer is small.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you never guess this 1 birthday number? | Wait for the last part. The answer is small. | [pause 0.5] | How many people must stand in one room? | We want a fair chance that two share a birthday. | It sounds like you need a very big crowd. | [pause 1.0] | You only need twenty-three people! | [pause 1.0] | That is because every pair of people counts. | That makes two hundred fifty-three possible pairs. | What number did you guess?
Frame 0: A party room, one guest, a counter, Spark holding a calendar with 365 on it
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark bets it takes 180 guests. Mr. Trick opens the door to guest 23 and rings a bell.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The number: twenty-three.
Reveal: Lines draw between every pair of guests until the room is a dense web of 253 lines.
Claim + numbers: 23 people: 50.73% (assumes 365 equal days). Pairs: 253. Both computed and checked.
Caveat: Two people share with each other, not with you.

Title: Can your brain adopt a fake hand?
Hook (spoken): Why would your brain never doubt 1 fake hand?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. It takes only a paintbrush.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why would your brain never doubt 1 fake hand? | Wait for the last part. It takes only a paintbrush. | [pause 0.5] | Hide one real hand behind a small wall. | Then place a fake hand right in front of you. | A friend brushes both hands at the same moment. | [pause 1.0] | The touch can feel like it is on the fake hand! | [pause 1.0] | Your brain joins what you see with what you feel. | It does not work on everyone. | Would you try this at home?
Frame 0: A rubber hand on a table, Spark looking at it with love; a wall hides his own hand
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick brushes both. Spark names the fake hand and refuses to give it back.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Spark says Ouch for the fake hand.
Reveal: The wall lifts: his real hand was there all along, and Spark looks shocked at it.
Comment question: Would you try this at home?
Claim + numbers: Botvinick & Cohen 1998: 10 subjects; 8 of 10 reported it (secondhand).
Caveat: Not everyone feels it. No number on screen unless the primary is opened.

Title: Have you seen a clock stop when you look at it?
Hook (spoken): Why do you see 1 clock stop when you look?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. The clock did nothing wrong.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you see 1 clock stop when you look? | Wait for the last part. The clock did nothing wrong. | [pause 0.5] | Look away from a clock, then look back quickly. | The first second can feel too long to you. | Scientists tested this with a small number counter. | [pause 1.0] | Less than one second felt like a full second! | [pause 1.0] | Your eyes jump, and your brain fills that moment. | Have you ever seen this happen to you?
Frame 0: A wall clock, second hand frozen mid-tick, Spark staring at it, one brow up
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark runs to complain to the shop that sold it. Mr. Trick shows him it is fine.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The viewer recognises the feeling.
Reveal: Timeline: the eye jump, then the moment that stretches, the extra fraction shown by a bar.
World: Clock repair shop with many clocks
Comment question: Have you ever seen this happen?
Claim + numbers: Yarrow 2001: n=30; digit judged equal to 1 s when seen 880 ms (22° jump) or 811 ms (55°).
Caveat: Lab counter test, not a wall clock.
Flags: Never say time stops. Do not state the brain's filling-in as certain.

Title: Can one short text describe you perfectly?
Hook (spoken): How can 1 short text describe you so well?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. It is not magic.

It is not magic. | [pause 0.5] | You want other people to like you very much. | You can be quite hard on yourself sometimes. | You have strengths that you do not use yet. | [pause 1.0] | A teacher gave these words to every student! | [pause 1.0] | They rated it over four out of five. | So be careful with fortune tellers and online tests. | Did that text fit you?
Frame 0: A paper with YOU at the top, handed straight to the camera; Spark astonished, reading it
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick, as a fortune teller, gives Spark his reading. Spark cries, it is so true. Then every student opens the same page.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The viewer feels described.
Reveal: A whole classroom holds up the same page, all reading the same words.
World: Purple fortune tent, then a classroom
Claim + numbers: Forer: same text for all students, mean 4.26 of 5 (secondhand).
Caveat: Published 1949. Say over four, not an exact figure.
Flags: Find Forer's paper on the day if possible.

Title: Have you ever seen your own eyes move?
Hook (spoken): Why have you never seen your 2 eyes move?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. Any mirror can prove it.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why have you never seen your 2 eyes move? | Wait for the last part. Any mirror can prove it. | [pause 0.5] | Stand close to a mirror, and look at one eye. | Now look quickly at your other eye. | [pause 2.5] | Your eyes moved, but you did not see them! | [pause 1.0] | A friend standing beside you can see them jump. | Your brain turns vision down during these fast jumps. | Use a mirror, because a phone camera has a delay. | Did you see your eyes move?
Frame 0: Spark nose-to-nose with his mirror image, both eyes wide
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark tries to catch his eyes moving, faster and faster. A friend beside him laughs.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Nothing moves in the mirror.
Reveal: Friend's view: the eyes clearly jump. The mirror's view: still.
Claim + numbers: Suppression during eye jumps is partial, about 3-10× (secondary).
Caveat: Partial suppression. Not blindness. The mirror demo is a secondhand classic.

Title: Does time really slow down when you are scared?
Hook (spoken): Does time stop for you in 1 scary fall?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. Scientists dropped people to check.
Voice script (rows split by |): Does time stop for you in 1 scary fall? | Wait for the last part. Scientists dropped people to check. | [pause 0.5] | Volunteers fell from a tall tower into a net. | They wore a watch that flashed numbers too fast. | If time slowed, they could read those numbers. | [pause 1.0] | They could not read them any better! | [pause 1.0] | But they remembered the fall as much longer. | So fear stretches the memory, not the moment. | Did time ever slow down for you?
Frame 0: Spark falling backward from a tower, watch on his wrist, mouth open
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick pushes the button. Spark screams, swears the fall lasted a week.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The test is set up: a watch flashing numbers too fast to read.
Reveal: Watch: nobody reads it better. Then the memory stretches out, like a long film strip beside a short real one.
Comment question: Did time ever slow down for you?
Claim + numbers: Stetson 2007: 2.49 s fall; estimates rose 36% over others' falls; in-flight reading no better than ground.
Caveat: Very small sample. No height on screen, because the paper is inconsistent.
Flags: Show a net and clearly safe set-up. No dare to imitate.

Title: Did Cambridge really prove you can read mixed-up words?
Hook (spoken): Why did you never doubt this 1 famous email?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. A real scientist checked.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why did you never doubt this 1 famous email? | Wait for the last part. A real scientist checked. | [pause 0.5] | Read this mixed-up sentence, and it still makes sense. | A famous email said Cambridge researchers proved this. | A Cambridge scientist looked, and knew of no such study. | [pause 1.0] | Salt and slat share their first and last letters! | [pause 1.0] | So the other letters matter, and mixed words slow you. | Did you believe that email?
Frame 0: Mixed-up sentence on a phone, Spark reading it easily, showing off
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark forwards the famous email to everyone. Mr. Trick pushes the real letter from the scientist in front of him.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The viewer reads it easily.
Reveal: SALT and SLAT side by side: same first letter, same last letter, and two different words.
Claim + numbers: Davis: knows of no one at Cambridge UK researching it; 'only first and last' is clearly wrong; 11% reading slowdown (Rayner, via Davis).
Caveat: You often can read them, so this is not 'all false'.
Flags: Do not name Davis in the hook.

Title: Why does this face look fine upside down?
Hook (spoken): Why do you miss what is wrong with 1 face?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. It will surprise you.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you miss what is wrong with 1 face? | Wait for the last part. It will surprise you. | [pause 0.5] | Look at this upside down face for a moment. | Does anything look wrong with it to you? | [pause 1.5] | Now I will slowly turn the picture around. | [pause 1.0] | The eyes and mouth were flipped the whole time! | [pause 1.2] | People rate it as far less strange upside down. | Scientists still debate why this happens. | Did you see that coming?
Frame 0: An upside-down invented face, smiling calmly; Spark tilting his whole body to look
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick hangs the portrait. Spark says it is lovely and rotates it, then jumps out of his sneakers.

Reveal: The face rotates slowly upright and turns monstrous, and Spark screams.

Caveat: Not 'totally normal' upside down. Explanation disputed.

Title: Can you spot the fake coin flips?
Hook (spoken): Why will you fail to spot 1 fake coin row?

The answer looks wrong. | [pause 0.5] | Row A keeps switching between heads and tails. | Row B has five heads all in a row. | Which row did a human make up? | [pause 1.5] | Row A is the fake row! | [pause 1.0] | People switch too often when they fake coin flips. | In a hundred real flips, that long streak is very likely. | Which row did you pick?

Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick flips real coins, Spark fakes his row, and Spark is certain he made the real-looking one.

Title: Can you make these colours vanish?
Hook (spoken): Stare 10 seconds. Why do these colours disappear?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. Do not move your eyes.
Voice script (rows split by |): Stare 10 seconds. Why do these colours disappear? | Wait for the last part. Do not move your eyes. | [pause 0.5] | Look only at the small dot in the centre. | [pause 7.5] | Are the soft colours starting to fade away now? | [pause 1.0] | Those colours never left your screen! | [pause 0.8] | Your brain can ignore things that do not change. | Move your eyes a little, and they come back. | Did the colours fade for you?
Frame 0: Soft colour blobs around one small dot, Spark at the edge, one finger up: shh
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark goes to steal the blobs while the viewer is staring. Mr. Trick is sneaking too.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The colours fade.
Reveal: A blink, and everything returns; a tag says THEY NEVER LEFT.
Comment question: Did the colours fade for you?
Claim + numbers: Blurry, low-contrast shapes can fade with steady gaze; small eye movements bring them back.
Caveat: Say can fade. Not everyone sees it fast.
Flags: Picture must be fully static during the stare, except Spark outside the shapes? Test: if Spark distracts, hide him. Owner tests on a real phone.

Title: Why does the small box feel heavier?
Hook (spoken): Why does 1 small box fool you every time?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. Knowing the truth does not help.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why does 1 small box fool you every time? | Wait for the last part. Knowing the truth does not help. | [pause 0.5] | These two boxes weigh exactly the same. | But lift them, and the small one feels heavier. | Your brain expects a big box to be heavy. | [pause 1.0] | Now you know they match, so lift them again. | [pause 1.0] | The small box still feels heavier to you! | Scientists have studied this for over a hundred years. | Which box would you pick up?
Frame 0: Big box and small box on a scale, level; Spark straining at the small one
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark picks up the big one easily, then almost drops the small one. Mr. Trick shows the scale, and Spark lifts again, still fooled.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The scale says equal.
Reveal: Spark knows the truth, tries again, and his arm still drops.
Claim + numbers: Size-weight illusion (Charpentier 1891): persists when you know; expectations explain about half.
Caveat: Cause not fully settled; say expects as part of why.

Title: Do people notice you as much as you think?
Hook (spoken): Why do you think everyone saw your 1 mistake?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. One silly shirt proved it.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why do you think everyone saw your 1 mistake? | Wait for the last part. One silly shirt proved it. | [pause 0.5] | Students wore an embarrassing shirt into a full room. | Then they guessed how many people noticed the shirt. | They guessed far more people than really noticed. | [pause 1.0] | Only about one person in four noticed it! | [pause 1.0] | You are the centre of your own world only. | So that mistake is smaller than it feels. | What embarrassed you this week?
Frame 0: Spark in a silly shirt, face red, a room of people; a big spotlight on him
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick gives Spark the shirt, Spark walks in sweating. The spotlight is only in his head.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Spark guesses half the room noticed.
Reveal: Spotlight switches off: most of the room is on their phones, and only a few look up.
Claim + numbers: Actual about 23% (confirmed via Macrae et al. citation). Guess about 46% from a weak blog only.
Caveat: Open JPSP 78:211 before showing 46. About a quarter did notice.
Flags: Generic shirt, no real singer's face.

Title: Which way is this dancer turning for you?
Hook (spoken): Which way is she turning? Why does it switch?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. A famous claim is wrong.
Voice script (rows split by |): Which way is she turning? Why does it switch? | Wait for the last part. A famous claim is wrong. | [pause 0.5] | The internet says this shows your left or right brain. | But she is only a flat shadow on a wall. | A flat shadow has no depth, so both ways fit. | [pause 1.0] | Your brain just picks one direction for itself! | [pause 1.0] | I found no proof it shows your brain type. | Which way did she turn for you?
Frame 0: A silhouette dancer turning on a spot; Spark's head turning with her, dizzy
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick sells a BRAIN TYPE test. Spark takes it twice and gets opposite answers.
First payoff (by ~10 s): She flips direction for many viewers.
Reveal: Silhouette seen from the side turns into a flat shadow, showing no depth.
Comment question: Which way did she turn for you?
Claim + numbers: Ambiguous figure: viewing time 0.508 clockwise, 3.68 reversals a minute (n=24).
Caveat: The debunk is a neurologist's blog; no peer-reviewed test. Say no proof found, not disproven.
Flags: Draw a new figure from a true 3D orthographic spin, not Kayahara's art.

Title: Can a still picture start to move?
Hook (spoken): Stare 10 seconds before you see this picture move.
Promise line: Wait for the last part. The picture never moves.
Voice script (rows split by |): Stare 10 seconds before you see this picture move. | Wait for the last part. The picture never moves. | [pause 0.5] | Look only at the centre while the wheel turns. | [pause 10.0] | Now look at this still picture of Spark. | [pause 2.0] | He is not moving, but your brain says he is! | [pause 0.8] | Your brain got used to that motion. | Did the picture move for you?
Frame 0: A slow, soft turning pattern with a centre dot, Spark at the side with his eyes closed
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick sets the wheel turning. Spark stares too long, and everything he looks at wobbles.
First payoff (by ~10 s): After the stare, Spark's still picture appears to drift.
Reveal: A label: THIS PICTURE IS NOT MOVING, while the viewer sees it drifting.
World: Pottery studio with a turning wheel
Comment question: Did the picture move for you?
Claim + numbers: Steady motion leaves a drift the other way. Studies used 4-30 s of adaptation.
Caveat: Stop if it feels uncomfortable (small line on screen).
Flags: SAFETY: slow, low contrast, 5 or fewer bands, no flash, no reversal, no saturated red. Owner tests before posting. Skip if in doubt.

Title: Can you answer this easy question?
Hook (spoken): Why will you probably fail this 1 easy question?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. It has only two answers.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why will you probably fail this 1 easy question? | Wait for the last part. It has only two answers. | [pause 0.5] | Linda cares about fairness and joins protest marches. | Is she a bank worker, or a bank worker and feminist? | [pause 2.5] | The first answer is always more likely! | [pause 1.0] | The second answer needs two things to be true. | In one study, most students chose the second answer. | Some say they read likely as fits the story. | Which answer did you pick?
Frame 0: Two cards A and B, Spark slapping B, certain
Spark + Mr. Trick: Mr. Trick tells the story of Linda. Spark falls for it, loudly.
First payoff (by ~10 s): Most pick B.
Reveal: Two circles: all bank tellers, and inside it the smaller group. B can never be larger.
Claim + numbers: 85% of 142 UBC undergraduates chose the conjunction.
Caveat: Debated: frequency wording reduces it, and people may read 'probable' differently.
Flags: Keep the tone neutral.

Title: Can you beat your first answer?
Hook (spoken): Why does your first answer fail this 1 puzzle?
Promise line: Wait for the last part. The answer is one day away.
Voice script (rows split by |): Why does your first answer fail this 1 puzzle? | Wait for the last part. The answer is one day away. | [pause 0.5] | Lily pads on a lake double every single day. | They cover the whole lake in forty-eight days. | So when did they cover half of the lake? | [pause 2.5] | It is not day twenty-four at all! | [pause 1.0] | It is day forty-seven, because they double once more. | Your fast answer often speaks before you check it. | What was your first answer?
Frame 0: A lake with one lily pad doubling, Spark standing on a pad, about to sink
Spark + Mr. Trick: Spark shouts 24! and steps forward. The lake stays half empty beneath him and he falls in.
First payoff (by ~10 s): The fast answer is wrong.
Reveal: Time runs backward from a full lake: one day back, and it is exactly half.
World: Green lake, camera rising from one pad to the whole lake
Claim + numbers: Cognitive Reflection Test item (Frederick 2005). Answer 47 by logic.
Caveat: Do not show a percentage wrong. Many people have seen it before.
